title: Network Access Control
summary: Network Access Control is the set of mechanisms that decide whether a device is allowed to join a network segment and what it may reach once joined, enforced at the point of connection: a switch port, a wireless association, or a virtual private network concentrator. A typical deployment uses port-based access control described by the IEEE 802.1X standard, where the switch acts as an authenticator, the device runs a supplicant, and a central server such as a RADIUS server validates credentials using a method like EAP-TLS with a certificate. Beyond admission, posture checks can inspect patch level, disk encryption or agent presence, and a device that fails can be placed in a restricted quarantine segment with only remediation resources. It also appears as guest onboarding portals and as device profiling that classifies unknown hardware. The recurring mistake is to treat admission as the end of the story: once a port is open, flat layer-two networks and weak internal segmentation let an admitted but compromised laptop reach everything, so 802.1X without micro-segmentation, and without monitoring of the MAC authentication bypass path used by printers and cameras, provides far less isolation than teams assume.

beginner.definition: Network access control is the system that checks a device before letting it join a network. It decides who may connect, and what they may reach after they connect. It is used on wired switch ports, on wireless networks and on remote access connections. Some products also check that the device is healthy before allowing it in.
beginner.whyItMatters: An open network port is an open door, and anyone who finds one can often reach servers inside. Guests and personal laptops can carry malware that spreads to the whole building. If a device is out of date or unprotected, letting it join puts everyone else at risk. Access control gives you a record of which device connected where and when. The risk of ignoring it is a network with no real defence. An outsider only needs to find the way in.
howItWorks: A device plugs into a switch port or joins a wireless network and asks to connect.
Until it proves itself, the switch allows only a small set of authentication traffic.
The device proves its identity with a password or, better, a certificate.
A central server checks those credentials and sends a decision back to the switch.
The switch then places the device in the right network group, or in a restricted quarantine area.
Optional health checks can limit access further until the device meets your rules.
beginner.example: Picture an airport with two doors. First you queue at the boarding gate. Staff check your ticket and passport, which is like proving identity to join. Then you may enter only the gate area on your own ticket, which is like your network group. A passenger who fails the check waits in a side room instead of boarding. Checking the ticket matters, but it does not help if every gate leads to the same plane.
takeaways: Access control answers two questions: may this device connect, and what may it reach afterwards.
Certificate based checks are stronger than shared passwords because each device has its own identity.
Admission alone is not isolation, so keep internal segments separated as well.

objectives: Explain the purpose of network access control and the decisions it makes at connection time.
Describe the roles of supplicant, authenticator and authentication server in port-based access control.
Compare password based and certificate based device authentication for network admission.
Discuss how quarantining devices that fail a health check limits damage while allowing repair.
Explain why admission control must be combined with internal segmentation to be effective.
